title: Floating and sinking: why a heavy rolling pin floats and a light coin sinks

summary.text: A heavy wooden rolling pin floats in a bucket of water, but a light one-rupee coin sinks. Your child guesses first, then tests ten things from the kitchen to see which float and which sink. They find that how heavy or how big a thing is does not decide it. A tiny piece of potato sinks, just like the whole potato. What a thing is made of, and whether it holds air inside, decides if it floats.
summary.art: A steel bucket of water on a kitchen floor, with a wooden rolling pin and a lemon floating on top, and a one-rupee coin, a steel spoon and a potato lying on the bottom.

intro.hook: Hold a wooden rolling pin in one hand and a one-rupee coin in the other. Which one is heavier? Now guess: which one will sink in a bucket of water?
intro.text: Most people guess that the heavy rolling pin will sink and the light coin will float. You are going to drop them in and see. Then you will test many more things from the kitchen. If weight does not decide what sinks, what does? This unit answers that question, and your own test will show you.
intro.art: A child holding a wooden rolling pin in one hand and a small coin in the other, looking at a bucket of water, with a thinking bubble showing the rolling pin at the bottom.

outcomes: By the end I can say what float and sink mean, and test a thing to find out which it does.
By the end I can make a guess before a test and give a reason for it.
By the end I can show that a heavy thing can float and a light thing can sink.
By the end I can show that a big piece and a small piece of the same material both float, or both sink.
By the end I can say that water pushes up on things put into it, and that air inside a thing helps it float.
By the end I can name things around me in India that float or sink, and say why.

terms.meaning: A thing floats when it stays at the top of the water. If you push it under and let go, it comes back up.
terms.example: A lemon floats in a bucket of water. Push it down, let go, and it bobs back up.
terms.art: A lemon bobbing on top of water in a steel bucket, with a finger just letting go of it.

terms.meaning: A thing sinks when it goes down to the bottom of the water and stays there.
terms.example: A one-rupee coin sinks to the bottom of a bucket.
terms.art: A coin falling through water and lying on the bottom of a bucket.

terms.meaning: A prediction is a guess about what will happen, made before you test it, with a reason.
terms.example: Nila predicts: 'The potato will sink, because it feels heavy and hard.'
terms.art: A girl pointing at a potato next to a bucket, with a speech bubble saying 'It will sink, because...'.

terms.meaning: A test is when you try something to find out what really happens.
terms.example: Putting the potato in the water is the test. It shows if your prediction was right.
terms.art: A hand lowering a potato into a bucket of water.

terms.meaning: A material is what a thing is made of, such as wood, steel, plastic or wax.
terms.example: A rolling pin is made of wood. A spoon is made of steel.
terms.art: A wooden rolling pin, a steel spoon, a plastic bottle cap and a wax candle in a row, each with a label.

terms.meaning: Upthrust is the push of water upwards on anything put into it. You can feel it when you push a ball down into water.
terms.example: Push a ball into a bucket. The water pushes it back up. That push is upthrust.
terms.art: A child's hands pushing a ball down into a bucket, with an arrow in the water pointing up.

terms.meaning: An air space is a tiny gap filled with air inside a thing. Many air spaces make a thing lighter for its size.
terms.example: An apple has lots of air spaces inside, so it floats.
terms.art: An apple cut in half, with a zoom circle showing tiny air gaps between the cells.

explanations.context: This card explains the two words we use when we put things in water.
explanations.definition: A thing floats if it stays at the top of the water and comes back up when you push it under and let go. A thing sinks if it goes to the bottom and stays there.
explanations.description: In the bucket test, you pushed each thing under with a finger, then let go. The lemon and the rolling pin came back up, so they float. The coin, the spoon and the potato stayed on the bottom, so they sink. Some floaters ride high, like a plastic bottle cap. Some float low, with most of their body under water, like an apple or an ice cube. Both are floating.
examples: A lemon bobs back up when you let go, so it floats.
A steel spoon stays at the bottom, so it sinks.
An ice cube floats, but most of it stays under the water.
explanations.art: A bucket cut away to show a bottle cap floating high, an ice cube floating low, and a spoon on the bottom.

explanations.context: This card explains the biggest surprise of the bucket test: the heavy rolling pin floated and the light coin sank.
explanations.definition: A heavy thing can float, and a light thing can sink. How heavy a thing feels in your hand does not tell you if it will float.
explanations.description: In your hand, the wooden rolling pin felt much heavier than the coin. Many children guess the rolling pin will sink. But in the bucket, the rolling pin floated and the coin sank. A big log floats down a river, while a small stone sinks. A huge ship floats, while a tiny steel pin sinks. So we cannot tell by weight alone.
examples: A wooden rolling pin is heavy and floats.
A one-rupee coin is light and sinks.
A whole coconut is heavy and floats.
explanations.art: A balance with a rolling pin on the heavy, low side and a coin on the light, high side, and beside it a bucket with the rolling pin floating and the coin on the bottom.

explanations.concept: What it is made of decides
explanations.context: This card explains what happened when we cut a potato small, and tried a tiny piece of wood.
explanations.definition: For a solid lump of one material, what the material is decides if it floats. A big piece and a small piece of the same material do the same thing.
explanations.description: The whole potato sank. A grown-up cut off a piece as small as your fingernail, and that sank too. The big wooden rolling pin floated, and so did a tiny matchstick. Think of a piece of wood and the same amount of water, the very same size and shape. The wood is lighter than that water, so it floats. A piece of steel is heavier than the same amount of water, so it sinks. Potato is a little heavier than water, so every piece of potato sinks.
examples: A whole potato and a tiny piece of potato both sink.
A big rolling pin and a small matchstick, both wood, both float.
A steel spoon and a steel key both sink.
explanations.art: Two rows in a bucket: a whole potato and a tiny potato piece on the bottom, and a rolling pin and a matchstick floating on top.

explanations.context: This card explains what you felt when you pushed a ball down into the bucket.
explanations.definition: Water pushes up on anything put into it. This push is called upthrust.
explanations.description: When you pushed the ball down, you felt the water pushing back. The deeper you pushed it, the harder the water pushed. When you let go, the ball jumped up. Water pushes up on a coin too, but the push is too small to hold the coin up, so the coin sinks. A thing floats when the push of the water is enough to hold up its whole weight.
examples: A ball pushed under water jumps back up when you let go.
Your arm feels lighter when you lift it in a bucket of water.
A coin gets a tiny push up, but not enough, so it sinks.
explanations.art: A ball held under water in a bucket by two small hands, with a big arrow under the ball pointing up.

explanations.context: This card explains the orange test, and why apples float.
explanations.definition: Air is very light. A thing with lots of air inside it is light for its size, so it is more likely to float.
explanations.description: An orange peel is full of tiny pockets of air. With its peel on, the whole orange floats. Peeled, the orange usually sinks. An apple floats because it has many air spaces between its cells. Thermocol is mostly air, so it floats very high. A life jacket is full of foam with air in it, so it helps a person float.
examples: A whole orange floats, and a peeled orange usually sinks.
An apple floats because of the air spaces inside it.
Thermocol is mostly air, and it floats high.
explanations.art: An orange with its peel floating, and a peeled orange on the bottom of a glass bowl of water, with a zoom circle showing air pockets in the peel.

explanations.concept: Another way to stay on top: the skin of water
explanations.context: This card is about a different reason some small things can rest on water.
explanations.definition: The top of water holds together like a very thin, stretchy skin. Very small, light things can rest on this skin without floating in the usual way.
explanations.description: If you lay a steel pin very gently on still water, it can rest on top. Push it, and it sinks, because steel is heavier than water. The skin of water held it up, not upthrust. Agnes Pockels, a woman in Germany, studied this skin in her own kitchen with a tray of water and a button. She had not been allowed to study at a university. In 1891, the famous science journal Nature printed her letter about it. That is why, in the bucket test, we push each thing under and let go.
examples: A steel pin laid gently on still water can rest on top.
Pond skaters, insects that walk on ponds, stand on the skin of the water.
explanations.art: A steel pin resting on the surface of water in a steel bowl, with the water surface dipping a little under it.

agreed.text: A thing floats or sinks depending on what it is made of, and on any air inside it, not on how heavy or how big it is.
agreed.evidence: In the bucket test, the heavy rolling pin floated, the light coin sank, and a tiny piece of potato sank like the whole potato.

agreed.text: Water pushes up on everything put into it. This push is called upthrust.
agreed.evidence: You can feel it when you push a ball down into water, and see it when you let go and the ball jumps up.

agreed.text: Air inside a thing makes it lighter for its size, and helps it float.
agreed.evidence: A whole orange floats, and the same orange usually sinks once its air-filled peel is taken off.

how_we_found_out.story: About 2,250 years ago, Archimedes lived in Syracuse, a Greek city on the island of Sicily. Many people then, and many people now, thought heavy things sink and light things float. But a big, heavy log floats, while a small pebble sinks. Archimedes worked out a better rule, and wrote it in a book called On Floating Bodies. He said a thing sinks into the water until it has pushed aside water as heavy as itself. A floating log pushes aside its own weight of water while part of it is still above the top. A pebble pushes aside all the water it can and is still heavier, so it sinks. His book was nearly lost. In the year 1229, someone scraped the writing off the old pages and wrote prayers over them. In 1906, the Danish scholar Johan Ludvig Heiberg found the faint old words under the prayers. Years later, a team at the Walters Art Museum in Baltimore, in the United States, read even more of the hidden writing. Abigail Quandt, a book expert there, spent years taking the crumbling pages apart safely.
how_we_found_out.who: Archimedes of Syracuse, and the people who saved his book: Johan Ludvig Heiberg, and Abigail Quandt and her team at the Walters Art Museum
how_we_found_out.when: About 250 BCE (the book), 1229 (written over), 1906 (found again), from 1999 (read again)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That heavy things sink and light things float. Archimedes showed that what matters is how heavy a thing is compared with the water it pushes aside, so a heavy log can float and a small pebble can sink.
how_we_found_out.art: An old man in a Greek tunic watching a log float and a pebble sink in a stone basin of water, and beside it an old book with faint Greek writing under newer lines.

challenging.claim: Heavy things sink and light things float.
challenging.who: A very common guess, by children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Many heavy things do sink, like a brick or a steel vessel full of water. Many light things float, like a leaf or a feather.
challenging.against: A heavy wooden rolling pin floats and a light coin sinks. A big ship floats. What a thing is made of, and the air inside it, matters more than its weight.
challenging.context: This card is about the guess most people make before the bucket test.

challenging.claim: Big things sink and small things float.
challenging.for: Big things are often heavier, so people expect them to sink.
challenging.against: A tiny piece of potato sinks just like the whole potato, and a tiny matchstick floats just like a big rolling pin. Size does not decide.
challenging.context: This card is about a guess that the potato test checks.

challenging.claim: Archimedes worked out his idea in the bath, and ran through the streets shouting 'Eureka!', which means 'I have found it!'
challenging.who: A famous story, first written by the Roman writer Vitruvius about 200 years after Archimedes died
challenging.for: The story is old, and it fits Archimedes, who did write a real book about floating.
challenging.against: Nobody wrote it down while Archimedes was alive. Historians are not sure it happened the way the story says.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous story you may hear about Archimedes.

big_questions.q: The rolling pin felt heavy in your hand, yet it floated. Why do our hands guess wrong about floating?
big_questions.hint: Your hand feels how heavy the whole thing is. Does it feel how heavy it is for its size?

big_questions.q: A peeled orange sinks and a whole orange floats. Is the peel part of the orange, or is it the orange's boat?
big_questions.hint: What is inside the peel that the juicy part does not have?

big_questions.q: When you are in water, you float a little better after a big breath in. What does that tell you about your own body?
big_questions.hint: Where does the air go when you breathe in?

big_questions.q: Coconuts can float across the sea to new islands and grow there. How do you think plants that cannot float travel to new places?
big_questions.hint: Think of seeds that fly, seeds that stick to fur, and seeds that birds eat.

big_questions.q: We guess before we test. Why is it worth guessing, if the test will show us the answer anyway?
big_questions.hint: What did you learn when your guess was wrong?

story.title: The Coconut That Would Not Sink
story.note: Kanji is rice cooked soft in plenty of water, eaten in Kerala, often on rainy days. Ammamma and Appooppa are Malayalam words for a mother's mother and a mother's father. Nila, Hari and their grandparents are made up.
text: It was raining hard in Kochi. Nila was seven, and her little brother Hari was five. They could not go out, so Ammamma, their grandmother, gave them a job.
"Wash the rice for the kanji," she said. She put a steel vessel of rice and water in front of them on the kitchen floor.
Hari swished the rice with his hand. Little brown flakes rose to the top and floated there.
"Those are husks," said Ammamma. "They are the thin dry coats of the rice. Scoop them off."
"The husks float because they are light," said Hari. "Light things float. Heavy things sink. Everyone knows that."
Nila looked at the rice grains lying on the bottom. One grain was much lighter than her hand. Yet it sank.
"Is that really true?" she asked.
Ammamma smiled. She took a big steel bucket and filled it half full with water from the tap. "Let us find out," she said. "But first, each of you must guess. And you must say why."
She put a row of things on the floor. There was a wooden rolling pin, a one-rupee coin, a lemon, a potato, a steel spoon and a whole coconut with its brown hair still on.
Hari picked up the coconut. It was the heaviest thing in the row. He needed both hands.
"The coconut will sink," he said, "because it is so heavy. And the coin will float, because it is so small."
Nila held the rolling pin in one hand and the coin in the other. The rolling pin was much heavier. "I think the rolling pin will sink," she said slowly. "But I am not sure."
"Good," said Ammamma. "Now test."
Hari dropped the coin in first. It wobbled down through the water and landed on the bottom with a little click.
Hari frowned.
Nila laid the rolling pin on the water. It dipped down, then rolled over and floated.
"It floated!" said Nila. "The heavy one floated, and the light one sank."
Then Hari lifted the big coconut and let it go. Splash! It went under, then bobbed straight back up and floated, turning slowly.
Hari's mouth fell open. "But it is so heavy," he said.

"Coconuts float very well," said Ammamma. "A coconut can float across the sea for weeks. When she lands on a new beach, she can grow into a new palm. That is how coconut palms reached many far islands."
They tried the rest. The lemon floated. The spoon sank. The potato sank.
"Maybe the potato is too big," said Hari. "A tiny piece will float."
"Guess first," said Nila. She was starting to like this game.
"A tiny piece will float," said Hari firmly.
Ammamma cut a piece of potato as small as Hari's fingernail. Hari dropped it in. It sank, just like the whole potato.
Nila thought hard. "So it is not how big it is," she said. "And it is not how heavy it is. It is what it is made of. Every piece of potato sinks. Wood floats, big or small."
To check, she found a used matchstick and put it on the water. The tiny stick floated, just like the big wooden rolling pin.
"Then why do the husks float?" asked Hari.
Nila picked one up and held it near the window. It was thin and dry, like paper. "Maybe husks are made of something lighter than water," she said. "Like the wood."
Just then, Appooppa, their grandfather, came in, shaking water off his umbrella.
Hari ran to him. "Appooppa, guess! Will this heavy rolling pin float or sink?"
"Sink, of course," said Appooppa. "It is heavy."
"Wrong!" said Hari. "Now guess the coin."
"The coin will float," said Appooppa. "It is so light."
Hari shook his head. He told Appooppa what Nila had found. It was not how heavy a thing was, and not how big. It was what the thing was made of.
Appooppa dropped the coin in, and it sank. He laughed. "I have lived for seventy years," he said, "and today a five-year-old taught me about floating."
"Nila taught me first," said Hari.
"And the bucket taught all of us," said Ammamma, and she put the rice on to cook.
story.epiphany: Whether a thing floats does not depend on how heavy or how big it is. A heavy rolling pin and a heavy coconut float, a light coin sinks, and a tiny piece of potato sinks like the whole potato. What a thing is made of decides. Guessing first, then testing, shows us when our guess was wrong.
ask: Why did Hari think the coconut would sink?
What did the tiny piece of potato show Nila?
Why did Ammamma make them guess before every test?
art: A rainy-day kitchen in Kochi, with a grandmother and two children kneeling around a steel bucket of water, a coconut floating in it and a coin on the bottom.
A grandfather with a wet umbrella laughing, as a small boy shows him a coin lying at the bottom of the bucket.

experiments.title: The Bucket Test: guess, then find out what floats
experiments.context: In this experiment you guess, then put ten things from the kitchen into a bucket of water, one at a time. You see which float and which sink. Then you test a tiny piece of potato and a tiny piece of wood.
experiments.question: Which things float and which sink? Do heavy things always sink, and do small things always float?
experiments.predict: Hold each thing in your hand. Will it float or sink? Why do you think so? Then guess: will a tiny piece of potato do the same as the whole potato, and why?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same bucket of water for every thing. We put each thing in gently, push it to the bottom with a finger, and let go. If it comes back up, it floats. If it stays down, it sinks. We test each thing twice, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: Heavy or light in my hand?

materials.item: a bucket or a big steel vessel, about half full of water
a wooden rolling pin (if yours is marble, steel or plastic, use a big wooden spoon)
a one-rupee coin, or any coin
a lemon
a raw potato
a steel spoon
a plastic bottle cap
an apple
a metal key
an ice cube
a short piece of candle
a used matchstick or a wooden toothpick
a knife and a cutting board, for a grown-up
a towel for drips, and paper and a pencil for the table

schedule.what: Feel each thing and guess. Test ten things in the bucket. Then test a tiny piece of potato and a matchstick. Count how many guesses were right.

experiments.record: Fill in the table as you go. At the end, draw the bucket with the floaters on top and the sinkers on the bottom. Count your right guesses with tally marks.

setup.art: A steel bucket half full of water on a towel on a kitchen floor, with a rolling pin, a coin, a lemon, a potato, a spoon, a bottle cap, an apple, a key, an ice cube and a candle in a row beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Fill a bucket half full. Line up the ten things.

setup.art: A child holding a rolling pin in one hand and a coin in the other, with a guess table on paper beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Feel each one. Guess float or sink, and say why.

setup.art: A finger pushing a lemon to the bottom of the bucket, and the lemon bobbing back up.
setup.caption: 3. Put it in. Push it down. Let go. Up or down?

setup.art: A grown-up cutting a fingernail-sized piece off a potato on a board, and the tiny piece lying on the bottom of the bucket.
setup.caption: 4. Test a tiny piece of potato and a matchstick.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bucket half full and put it on a towel. 2. Line up the ten things. 3. Your child holds each one, then sorts them into heavy and light.
flow.say: Hold each thing. Which feel heavy? Which feel light? Put the heavy ones on one side.
flow.kid: Hold each thing. Is it heavy or light? Make two piles.

ask.q: Which is heavier, the rolling pin or the coin?
good: The rolling pin, by a lot.

flow.parent: This step matters. Your child will use these feelings to guess. Write heavy or light in the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the bucket test. You feel how heavy each thing is.

flow.do: 1. Point to each thing in turn. 2. Your child says float or sink, and why. 3. Write each guess in the table.
flow.say: Now guess for each one. Will it float or sink? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess for each thing. Float or sink? Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think the rolling pin will sink?
good: Wood floats, so it will float.

flow.parent: Do not say if a guess is right. Most children say heavy things sink. Any guess with a reason is a good guess.
flow.context: In this step of the bucket test, you guess float or sink for each thing.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts in one thing at a time. 2. They push it to the bottom with a finger and let go. 3. Write what it did. 4. Take it out before the next one.
flow.say: Put it in gently. Now push it down to the bottom and let go. Did it come back up? Then it floats.
flow.kid: Put it in. Push it down. Let go. Did it come up?

ask.q: What did the rolling pin do?
good: It floated, even though it is heavy.

ask.q: What did the coin do?
good: It sank, even though it is light.

flow.parent: Pushing each thing down and letting go stops tiny things resting on the water's skin. Expect: rolling pin, lemon, bottle cap, apple, ice and candle float. Coin, potato, spoon and key sink. If a bottle cap fills with water, empty it and lay it flat side down.

check.q: The heavy rolling pin floated, and the light coin sank. What does that show?
options: How heavy a thing is does not decide if it floats
check.why: The rolling pin was much heavier, yet it floated. So weight alone does not decide. Picking 'heavy things always sink' means trusting the hand more than the test.

flow.context: In this step of the bucket test, you put each thing in the water and see if it floats.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts a piece of potato as small as a fingernail. 2. Your child guesses, then drops it in. 3. Then they guess and test a matchstick.
flow.say: The whole potato sank. Will a tiny piece float? Why do you think so? Now try it.
flow.kid: Guess: will a tiny piece of potato float? Say why. Now drop it in.

ask.q: What did the tiny piece of potato do?
good: It sank, like the whole potato.

ask.q: What did the matchstick do?
good: It floated, like the rolling pin.

flow.parent: Many children think a small piece will float. It sinks, because potato is a little heavier than the same amount of water. Push it down if it rests on the top.
flow.context: In this step of the bucket test, you check if a tiny piece does the same as a big piece.

flow.do: 1. Count the right guesses with tally marks. 2. Ask the questions below. 3. Listen before you explain.
flow.say: How many guesses were right? Which ones surprised you? So what decides if a thing floats?
flow.kid: Count your right guesses. Which ones surprised you? What decides if a thing floats?

ask.q: What decides if a thing floats?

flow.parent: After your child answers, say it plainly. Weight and size do not decide. For a solid lump, what it is made of decides. Wood is lighter than the same amount of water, so it floats. Steel and potato are heavier, so they sink.
flow.think: A steel spoon sinks. Do you think a steel bowl would sink too? Try it gently, and keep the water out.
flow.context: This is the last step of the bucket test. You count your right guesses and say what you found.

experiments.title: The Orange Test: does the peel help an orange float?
experiments.context: In this experiment you float a whole orange in water. Then you peel it and try again. You also float the peel on its own.
experiments.question: Does an orange float because of its peel?
experiments.predict: The whole orange floats. Will it still float without its peel? Will the peel float on its own? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same orange and the same bucket of water each time. We push it down and let go each time. We test the peeled orange three times, because it can float low and hard to judge.

materials.item: an orange, or a mosambi (sweet lime)
a bucket or a big clear bowl of water
a plate for the peel
a towel

schedule.what: Float the whole orange. Peel it. Guess, then test the peeled orange and the peel. Look at the peel closely.

experiments.record: Draw the whole orange, the peeled orange and the peel in the water, at the place each one ended up.

setup.art: A whole orange floating in a clear bowl of water.
setup.caption: 1. Float the whole orange.

setup.art: A child peeling an orange over a plate.
setup.caption: 2. Peel it. Guess what it will do now.

setup.art: A peeled orange lying on the bottom of the bowl, and pieces of peel floating on top.
setup.caption: 3. Test the peeled orange and the peel.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts the whole orange in the water. 2. They push it down and let go.
flow.say: Does the whole orange float or sink? Push it down and let go.
flow.kid: Put the orange in. Push it down. Let go. Float or sink?

ask.q: What does the whole orange do?
good: It floats low, with only the top showing.

flow.do: 1. Your child peels the orange over a plate. 2. They look at the inside of the peel. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Look at the inside of the peel. It is soft and spongy. Now guess. Will the peeled orange float? Why?
flow.kid: Peel the orange. Feel the soft white inside of the peel. Will the peeled orange float? Why?

ask.q: Will the peeled orange float?
good: Yes, because it is lighter now.
No, because the peel was helping.

flow.parent: Children often say it will float better, because it is lighter. Write the guess down.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts the peeled orange in and lets go. 2. Then they put in the pieces of peel. 3. Test the peeled orange three times.
flow.say: Put the peeled orange in. Push it down and let go. What happens? Now try the peel.
flow.kid: Put the peeled orange in. Let go. What happens? Now try the peel.

ask.q: What did the peeled orange do?
What did the peel do?

flow.parent: The peeled orange usually sinks slowly. If it still floats, peel off more of the white layer and try again. The peel floats because it is full of tiny pockets of air.

check.q: The whole orange floated, but the peeled orange sank. Why?
options: The peel is full of tiny air pockets, which helped it float
The orange got heavier when peeled
check.why: Peeling made the orange lighter, yet it sank. The peel holds lots of air, and air is very light. With its peel on, the orange is light for its size.

flow.do: 1. Ask the question below. 2. Then share the orange and eat it together.
flow.say: The peel made the orange lighter for its size. Why do you think a life jacket helps a person float?
flow.kid: Why does a life jacket help a person float? Now eat the orange.

ask.q: Why does a life jacket help a person float?
good: It is full of air, like the peel.
It is made of light foam.

flow.think: An apple floats with or without its skin. Where do you think an apple keeps its air?

activities.title: Heavy in the Hand: line up the kitchen
activities.context: In this activity you hold five things, one in each hand, and put them in a line from heaviest to lightest. You will use this line to make your guesses in the bucket test.

materials.item: a wooden rolling pin, a potato, a lemon, a steel spoon and a one-rupee coin

schedule.what: Hold the five things in pairs. Put them in a line from heaviest to lightest.

activities.record: Draw your line of five things, the heaviest first.

setup.art: A child holding a potato in one hand and a lemon in the other, arms out like a balance.
setup.caption: 1. Hold two things. Which is heavier?

setup.art: A rolling pin, a potato, a lemon, a spoon and a coin laid in a line on the floor from big to small.
setup.caption: 2. Line them up, heaviest first.

flow.do: 1. Give your child two things at a time, one for each hand. 2. They say which is heavier. 3. Swap until all five are compared.
flow.say: Hold one in each hand. Which one pulls your hand down more?
flow.kid: Hold one thing in each hand. Which is heavier?

ask.q: Which is the heaviest of all?

flow.parent: A wooden rolling pin and a potato are usually the heaviest. The coin is the lightest. Close eyes for a fairer feel, if your child likes.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts the five things in a line, heaviest first. 2. Ask the question below. 3. Leave the line out for the bucket test.
flow.say: Now look at your line. If heavy things sink, which ones will sink? Keep this line for the bucket test.
flow.kid: Look at your line. Which ones do you think will sink? Why?

ask.q: Which ones will sink?
good: The heavy ones, the rolling pin and the potato.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The bucket test will show that weight alone does not decide.

activities.title: What Floats in the Rice Water?
activities.context: In this activity you wash rice or dal before cooking, and look closely at what floats to the top. Then you check if the floaters are different from the grains that sank.

materials.item: a handful of rice, or a handful of dal such as toor dal or moong
a steel bowl of water
a spoon and a white plate
a magnifying glass, if you have one

schedule.what: Wash rice or dal. Scoop off what floats. Compare the floaters with the grains that sank.

activities.record: Draw a grain that sank and a bit that floated, side by side. Write one way they are different.

setup.art: A child swishing rice in a steel bowl of water, with tiny flakes floating on top.
setup.caption: 1. Swish the rice in water. Watch the top.

setup.art: A white plate with a few floating flakes on one side and full rice grains on the other.
setup.caption: 2. Scoop off the floaters. Compare them with the grains.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts the rice in the bowl of water. 2. They swish it with their hand. 3. Wait a few seconds, then look at the top.
flow.say: Swish the rice. Now look at the top of the water. Is anything floating?
flow.kid: Swish the rice in the water. Look at the top. What floats?

ask.q: What do you see on top?

flow.parent: Floaters are usually husk flakes, dust, broken bits or empty grains. Some rice has very few. That is a result too: it means the rice is clean and full.

flow.do: 1. Your child scoops the floaters onto the plate. 2. They put a few sunken grains beside them. 3. Look closely, with a magnifying glass if you have one.
flow.say: Put the floaters next to the grains that sank. How are they different?
flow.kid: Put the floaters next to the grains that sank. How are they different?

ask.q: Why do you think these bits floated?
good: They are thin and dry, like paper.

flow.parent: Farmers use the same idea to check seeds. Full, healthy seeds usually sink in water. Empty or damaged seeds float, because they hold air instead of food.

check.q: Some rice bits floated and most grains sank. What does that tell you?
options: The floaters are made differently, or hold air
The water pushed the grains down
check.why: A full grain is heavier than the same amount of water, so it sinks. A thin husk or an empty grain holds air and floats.

activities.title: Push It Down: feel the water push back
activities.context: In this activity you push a ball down into a bucket of water. You feel the water push back up, and watch the ball jump up when you let go.

materials.item: a bucket about three-quarters full of water
a plastic ball, or a small empty plastic box with its lid closed tight
a lemon
a towel for splashes

schedule.what: Push a lemon, then a ball, down into the water. Feel the push. Let go and watch.

activities.record: Draw the ball under the water with an arrow showing which way the water pushed.

setup.art: Two small hands pushing a plastic ball down into a bucket of water, with water splashing at the edges.
setup.caption: 1. Push the ball down slowly. Feel the water push back.

setup.art: A ball shooting up out of the water in a bucket, with drops flying.
setup.caption: 2. Let go. Watch the ball jump up.

flow.do: 1. Your child pushes the lemon down to the bottom with one finger. 2. Then they let go. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Push the lemon down with one finger. Do you feel anything pushing back? Now let go.
flow.kid: Push the lemon down. Feel it push back? Let go.

ask.q: What did you feel?
good: The lemon wanted to come up.

flow.do: 1. Your child pushes the ball down slowly with both hands. 2. They notice if the push gets stronger as it goes deeper. 3. They let go, keeping faces back from the splash.
flow.say: Push the ball down slowly. Is the push bigger than the lemon's? Does it get harder as you go deeper? Now let go.
flow.kid: Push the ball down slowly. Is it harder than the lemon? Let go and step back.

ask.q: Was the ball harder to push down than the lemon?
good: It got harder as it went deeper.

flow.parent: The push of water upwards is called upthrust. A big ball pushes a lot of water aside, so the water pushes back hard. Water pushes up on a coin too, but only a little, so the coin sinks.

check.q: Why did the ball jump up when you let go?
check.why: Water pushes up on anything put into it. This push is called upthrust. The push on the ball is much bigger than the ball's weight, so the ball shoots up.

games.title: Float or Sink? Guess, then flip
games.context: This is a guessing card game. Each card names a thing. You guess if it floats or sinks and say why, then flip the card to check.

printables.title: The two-zone board, drawn on a big sheet of paper
items: Bottom half, coloured brown, like the bottom of a bucket: SINK

items.b: Floats. Wood is lighter than the same amount of water.
Sinks. Steel is heavier than the same amount of water.
Floats. It bobs back up when you push it down.
Sinks. Even a tiny piece of potato sinks.
Floats. Coconuts can float across the sea to new islands.
Floats. Most of the ice stays under the water.
Sinks. Steel is heavier than the same amount of water.
Sinks. Metal is heavier than the same amount of water.
Sinks. Glass is heavier than the same amount of water.
Floats. An apple has lots of air spaces inside.
Floats very high. Thermocol is mostly air.
Floats. Its peel is full of tiny air pockets.
Usually sinks. Without the peel, it has lost its air pockets.
Floats, just like a big piece of wood.
Floats. Candle wax is lighter than the same amount of water.
Floats. Most bottle caps are made of a plastic lighter than water.

rules: Draw the board: a big sheet with FLOAT at the top and SINK at the bottom.
Shuffle the 16 cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns. Turn over the top card and read it out. Put it on FLOAT or SINK, and say why.
Then flip the card and read the back. A right guess with a reason scores one tally mark.
When all 16 cards are placed, count the tally marks. Playing alone, try to beat your own score next time.

setup.art: A big sheet of paper, blue on top labelled FLOAT and brown below labelled SINK, with a pile of small cards beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the board. Shuffle the cards.

setup.art: A child placing a card that says 'A whole coconut' on the FLOAT half and turning it over.
setup.caption: 2. Guess, say why, then flip to check.

flow.do: 1. Draw the board with your child. 2. Cut out the cards. 3. Read the first card together.
flow.say: Every card goes on float or sink. Before you put it down, say why you think so.
flow.kid: Draw the board. Cut out the cards. Read the first one.

flow.do: 1. Take turns with the cards. 2. The player places the card and gives a reason. 3. Flip it and score.
flow.say: A whole coconut. It is very heavy. Float or sink? Why?
flow.kid: Turn over a card. Float or sink? Say why. Then flip it.

ask.q: Why did you put the coconut on float?
good: It is like the rolling pin.

flow.parent: The coconut, the peeled orange and the coin catch most players out. Ask for the bucket test as evidence: 'What did the rolling pin do?'

flow.do: 1. Look at the sink cards together. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at all the sink cards. What are most of them made of?
flow.kid: Look at the sink cards. What are they made of?

ask.q: What are most of the sinkers made of?

games.title: Bob Up, Sink Down: a moving game
games.players: 2 or more players, with one caller
games.context: This is a moving game. The caller reads out a thing. The players stand up tall if it floats, or crouch down low if it sinks.

items.b: Float: stand up tall on tiptoe.
Sink: crouch down low and stay there.
Float: stand tall, even though coconuts are heavy.
Sink: crouch down low.
Start low, then spring up tall: a floater comes back up.
Sink: crouch low, just like a whole potato.
Float low: stand, but bend your knees. Most of the ice stays under water.
Float high: stand on tiptoe with arms up.
Sink slowly: crouch down very slowly.
Float: stand tall. The peel holds air.
Sink: crouch low.
Float: stand tall, just like the rolling pin.

rules: Clear a space in the room.
One person is the caller. Everyone else starts standing.
The caller reads the front of a card out loud. The players move: tall for float, low for sink.
The caller reads the back, so everyone can check. Anyone who moved the wrong way says why the card is right.
After 12 cards, a new player becomes the caller.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a card that says 'A coin!' while two children crouch down low.
setup.caption: 1. The caller reads a card.

setup.art: Two children springing up tall on tiptoe with arms raised.
setup.caption: 2. Stand tall for float. Crouch low for sink.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Clear a space. 3. Show the two moves.
flow.say: Floaters stand up tall. Sinkers crouch down low and stay there.
flow.kid: Float: stand tall. Sink: crouch low.

flow.do: 1. Read each card. 2. Wait for the players to move. 3. Read the back to check.
flow.say: A coconut! What do you do?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Stand tall or crouch low.
flow.parent: With only one child and one grown-up, the grown-up plays too, and the child is the caller for half the cards.

flow.do: 1. At the end, ask the question below.
flow.say: Which cards tricked you? Why?
flow.kid: Which cards tricked you? Why?

ask.q: Which card tricked you?
good: The coconut, because it is heavy.

challenges.title: Rescue the Coin: make a sinker float
challenges.context: This is a problem-solving challenge. A coin sinks. Your job is to make it float for a count of ten, without bending or breaking it.
challenges.problem: Put a one-rupee coin in a bucket of water, and it sinks. Find a way to make the coin stay at the top of the water while you count to ten.
constraints: Do not bend, cut or break the coin.
The coin must be at the top of the water, not held by your hand.
materials: sticky tape and a rubber band
things that float from the bucket test: a lemon, a bottle cap, a wooden rolling pin, a piece of thermocol, wooden ice-cream sticks
general: Tape the coin on top of a piece of thermocol, which floats very high.
Lay the coin on top of the floating wooden rolling pin.
creative: Tape the coin to a lemon. Does the lemon still float? Test it and see.
Put the coin in a small steel katori and float the katori. You will find out why a steel bowl floats in Class 4.
challenges.your_turn: Think of your own way. Test it. Then try to rescue two coins, then three. How many coins can your floater hold?

setup.art: A coin on the bottom of a bucket, and beside the bucket thermocol, a lemon, tape, ice-cream sticks and a steel katori.
setup.caption: 1. The coin sinks. Choose a floater to help it.

setup.art: A coin taped on a piece of thermocol floating on water, with a child counting on her fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Make the coin float. Count to ten.

flow.do: 1. Drop the coin in to show it sinks. 2. Read the rules together. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: The coin sinks on its own. What could hold it up? Think of the floaters from the bucket test.
flow.kid: The coin sinks. What could hold it up?

ask.q: What could you use?

flow.do: 1. Your child chooses a floater and fixes the coin to it. 2. They put it in the water and count to ten. 3. If it sinks, they try another way.
flow.say: Try your idea. Count to ten. If it sinks, what could you change?
flow.kid: Try your idea. Count to ten. Did the coin stay up?
flow.parent: Thermocol and the rolling pin always work. A lemon may or may not hold a coin, so it is a real test. Let your child try more than one way.

flow.do: 1. Ask the questions below. 2. Then try two or three coins.
flow.say: Which floater held the coin best? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which floater worked best? Why? Now try two coins.

ask.q: Why did the thermocol hold the coin up?
good: It floats very high, so it has push to spare.

flow.think: A big ship is made of steel, and steel sinks. What do you think holds a ship up?

items.p: Draw a line from each word to what it means.
pairs: stays at the top, and comes back up when pushed under
goes to the bottom and stays there
a guess with a reason, made before a test
items.why: These are the main words in this unit. A floater comes back up, a sinker stays down, and we guess before we test.

items.p: In the bucket test, which one floated?
items.why: The rolling pin floated, though it was the heaviest. Picking the coin may mean thinking light things always float.
items.context: This question is about the bucket test. You guess, then put ten things from the kitchen into a bucket of water, one at a time, to see which float and which sink.

items.p: Sort these into float and sink.
items.why: The lemon, ice and candle float. The key, potato and spoon sink. Metal and potato are heavier than the same amount of water.

items.p: Draw the bucket from your test. Draw the things that floated at the top, and the things that sank at the bottom.
items.a: A bucket with the rolling pin, lemon and other floaters at the top, and the coin, spoon and potato on the bottom.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the heavy rolling pin at the top and the light coin at the bottom, and labels them.
items.context: This question is about the bucket test. You guess, then put ten things from the kitchen into a bucket of water, one at a time, to see which float and which sink.
items.art: An outline of an empty bucket with a wavy line for the top of the water.

items.p: A small thing always floats.
items.why: False. A coin and a tiny piece of potato are small, and they sink. A small thing floats only if it is made of something lighter than water, like wood.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: the rolling pin felt heavy, yet it floated. Why?
items.a: Because it is made of wood. Wood is lighter than the same amount of water, so it floats, even when it is a big heavy piece.
items.why: A strong answer says that weight does not decide, and names the material, wood.
items.context: This question is about the bucket test. You guess, then put ten things from the kitchen into a bucket of water, one at a time, to see which float and which sink.

items.p: Priya guessed for 10 things in the bucket test. She got 6 right. How many did she get wrong?
items.why: 10 take away 6 is 4. A wrong guess is useful too: it shows where our first idea did not match what happened.

items.p: Label each picture: float or sink.
labels: a piece of thermocol in water
items.why: The coconut is heavy but floats. Thermocol is mostly air and floats very high. The coin sinks.
items.art: Three small pictures of a coconut, a coin and a piece of thermocol, each with an empty label line under it.

items.p: Sneha, aged 8, and her friend Bornali, aged 7, see a big wooden log floating in a river.

views.says: The log floats because it is big and wide. A small piece of the same wood would sink.
The log floats because it is made of wood. A small piece of the same wood would float too.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use something from your own bucket test as evidence. Then say one thing the other girl noticed that is worth checking.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Bornali and gives evidence: the tiny matchstick floated like the big rolling pin, and the tiny potato piece sank like the whole potato. It also says Sneha is right that shape can matter for some things, like a steel bowl, which is worth testing.
items.why: Both girls give a reason. The bucket test showed that for a solid lump, the material decides, not the size. Shape and air inside can matter for hollow things, which the Class 4 unit tests.

items.p: Three of these float. Which one sinks?
items.why: A glass marble sinks, because glass is heavier than the same amount of water. The other three float.

items.p: Kiran, a girl in Pune, wants to know if a tiny piece of potato floats. What should she do first?
items.why: First she guesses and gives a reason. Then the test shows if she was right. Guessing first helps her notice what surprised her.

items.p: The push of water upwards on anything put into it is called ________.
items.why: Upthrust is what you feel when you push a ball down into water. It is what holds floaters up.
items.context: This question is about pushing a ball down into a bucket of water and feeling the water push back.

items.p: In the orange test, what happened to the orange after it was peeled?
items.why: The peel is full of tiny air pockets. Without it, the orange is heavier than the same amount of water, so it usually sinks. Picking 'floated higher' means thinking lighter always floats.
items.context: This question is about the orange test. You float a whole orange, then peel it and try again.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why does a life jacket help a person float?
items.a: A life jacket is full of foam with air in it. Air is very light, so the person and the jacket together are light for their size, and they float.
items.why: A strong answer links the jacket to the orange peel or to thermocol: things full of air float.

items.p: Put the steps of a good test in order.
items: Put the thing in the water, push it down and let go
a: Put the thing in the water, push it down and let go
items.why: We guess first, so the test can show us if our idea was right. Then we test. Then we write it down, so we remember.

items.p: Draw a ball being pushed down into water. Draw an arrow to show which way the water pushes.
items.a: A ball under water, with hands on top, and an arrow pointing up from under the ball.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the arrow pointing up. That push is upthrust.
items.context: This question is about pushing a ball down into a bucket of water and feeling the water push back.
items.art: An outline of a bucket of water with a ball under the surface.

items.p: Two cooks are washing rice. Some flakes and grains float to the top.

views.who: Aunty Meera, a cook in Chennai
views.says: Scoop off the floaters and throw them away. They are husks and empty grains.

views.who: Fathima, aged 9, who loves to waste nothing
views.says: Keep the floating grains. They are rice too, so we should cook them.

items.ask: Whose plan would you choose? Give a reason. Then say what the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, such as 'floaters are often empty, so they have little food in them'. It also says what the other is right about, such as 'some floating grains may be fine, and wasting food is not good'.
items.why: Both have a point. Floating bits are often husk, dust or empty grains with little food. Some may be whole grains that held a bubble of air. Looking closely before throwing them away is fair to both views.
items.context: This question is about washing rice. You swish rice in water and look at what floats to the top.

items.p: Water pushes up on a coin, even though the coin sinks.
items.why: True. Water pushes up on everything put into it. The push on a coin is too small to hold up the coin's weight, so it sinks.

items.p: Mehak in Amritsar says: 'A tiny piece of potato will float, because it is so light.' What test would you show her, and what would she see?
items.a: Cut a tiny piece of potato and drop it in water. Push it down and let go. It sinks, just like the whole potato.
items.why: A strong answer describes a real test and says what happens. It shows that the material, not the size, decides.

items.p: Look at the apple cut in half. Label the part that helps it float.
labels: the tiny air spaces inside the apple
a: the tiny air spaces: they make the apple light for its size
items.why: An apple has many tiny air spaces between its cells. Air is very light, so the apple floats.
items.art: An apple cut in half, with a zoom circle on the white part showing tiny gaps, and one empty label line.

items.p: Lakshmi drops a big wooden block and a small wooden button into water. What will happen?
opts: The block sinks, the button floats
items.why: Both are made of wood, and wood is lighter than the same amount of water. Big or small, they both float. Picking 'the block sinks' means thinking big things sink.

items.p: In the bucket test, 6 things floated and 4 sank. How many things were tested in all?
items.why: 6 and 4 make 10. Counting floaters and sinkers helps us see that most of the kitchen things floated.
items.context: This question is about the bucket test. You guess, then put ten things from the kitchen into a bucket of water, one at a time, to see which float and which sink.

items.p: A coconut can float across the sea and grow on a new island. Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: how does floating help the coconut palm?
items.a: The coconut seed floats away to new beaches far away. There she can grow into a new palm, where no palm grew before.
items.why: A strong answer says floating carries the seed to new places to grow.

videos.why: Shows children guessing first, then testing everyday things in a tub of water.
videos.check: Not yet found. Search for a short float and sink video for ages 6 to 8 that pushes things under, and watch it first.

videos.title: Why does a peeled orange sink?
videos.why: Shows a whole orange floating and a peeled orange sinking, like our orange test.
videos.check: Not yet found. Search for the orange peel float test and check that it shows the peel floating alone.

videos.title: Coconuts at sea: how a seed travels by floating
videos.why: Shows coconuts floating on the sea and sprouting on a beach.
videos.check: Not yet found. Search for a nature video on coconut seed dispersal by sea, and check the facts the video gives.

opts: It goes to the bottom and stays there
It stays at the top and comes back up when pushed under
quiz.why: A floater stays at the top. Push it under, let go, and it comes back up. Picking 'goes to the bottom' mixes it up with sinking.
Steel is heavier than the same amount of water, so a steel spoon sinks. Wood and most bottle caps float.

quiz.p: Divya, a girl in Madurai, is about to test a cucumber. What is a good prediction?
opts: 'It will float, because it feels light for its size.'
quiz.why: A prediction is a guess with a reason. 'Let's see' is not a guess. 'It will float' has no reason.

quiz.p: A heavy rolling pin floated and a light coin sank. What does this show?
opts: Weight alone does not decide if a thing floats
quiz.why: If heavy things always sank, the rolling pin would have sunk. Weight alone does not decide.

quiz.p: A whole coconut is very heavy. In water, it...
quiz.why: A whole coconut floats, though it is heavy. Coconuts can float across the sea.

quiz.p: The whole potato sank. What does a tiny piece of the same potato do?
opts: It floats, because it is small
It sinks, just like the whole potato
quiz.why: Potato is a little heavier than the same amount of water, so every piece sinks. Picking 'floats' means thinking small things float.

quiz.p: Ayesha, a girl in Hyderabad, floats a big log of wood and a small twig of the same wood. What happens?
opts: The log floats, the twig sinks
quiz.why: Both are made of the same wood, so both float. Size does not decide.

quiz.p: You push a ball down into a bucket of water. What do you feel?
opts: The water pushing it back up
quiz.why: Water pushes up on anything put into it. This push is called upthrust.

quiz.p: Why does a whole orange float, when a peeled orange usually sinks?
opts: The peel is full of tiny air pockets
quiz.why: Air is very light. The peel's air pockets make the whole orange light for its size. Picking 'the peel is heavy' would mean the peeled orange should float better.

quiz.p: At Hogenakkal on the Kaveri river, people ride in round boats called coracles. Why do coracles float?
opts: They are made of light, woven bamboo with a waterproof cover, and hold air inside
The river is too shallow to sink in
quiz.why: Coracles are made of woven bamboo with a waterproof cover underneath. Bamboo floats, and the round bowl shape holds air above the water.

quiz.p: In the kitchen, which of these floats to the top when you wash rice?
opts: Thin dry husks and empty grains
quiz.why: Husks and empty grains are light for their size, or hold air, so they float. Full grains and stones sink.

applications: Farmers put seeds in water before sowing. Full, healthy seeds usually sink, and empty or damaged seeds float, so they can be taken out.
Fishers in Kerala, Odisha and Gujarat tie floats to the top edge of their nets, so the net hangs in the water like a curtain.
Life jackets are full of foam with air in it, so they help a person float.
Some recycling plants put chopped plastic in water. Some kinds of plastic float and others sink, so they can be sorted.
Many cooks check an egg by putting it in water. A fresh egg sinks. A very old egg may float, because air has got inside.

spotted.text: Kettuvallam houseboats, made of wood, floating on the backwaters of Alappuzha in Kerala.

spotted.text: Phumdis, floating islands of plants, soil and roots, on Loktak Lake in Manipur. Keibul Lamjao, a national park on the lake, floats on them, and the rare sangai deer live there.
spotted.art: Round green floating islands of grass on a wide lake, with a fisher's hut on one of them.

spotted.text: Clay Ganesha and Durga idols sinking in water after festivals in Mumbai and Kolkata. Clay is heavier than the same amount of water.
spotted.art: A clay idol being lowered gently into a tank of water by a family.

spotted.text: Fishing nets on a beach in Puri, Odisha, with a row of floats along the top edge.
spotted.art: A fishing net spread out on sand with a line of round floats along one edge.

spotted.text: Husks floating to the top when someone washes rice or dal in a steel vessel.
spotted.art: A hand swishing rice in a steel vessel, with little flakes floating on top.

open_questions.q: When did people first make boats or rafts?
open_questions.why_open: The oldest boat ever found is a dugout canoe about 10,000 years old, found in the Netherlands. But people reached Australia across the sea more than 50,000 years ago, so they must have floated on something much earlier. Those rafts were made of wood or plants that rotted away, so nobody knows what they looked like.

open_questions.q: How exactly do phumdis, the floating islands of Loktak Lake, form, and why are they changing?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know phumdis are mats of plants, roots and soil. But they still study how fast new ones form, and why many have grown thinner or moved since a dam was built on the lake in the 1980s.

ask_kids: What on your plate today would float? What would sink? How could you check?
Which do you think floats: a cucumber or a carrot? Why?
When you have a bath, does a full mug float or sink? What about an empty mug?
Why do you think boats are not made of potato?
What is something heavy that floats, that you have seen?

jokes.j: Why did the coin go to the bottom of the bucket?
jokes.a: It wanted to make a deep impression!

jokes.j: What did the lemon say when it was pushed under the water?
jokes.a: You can't keep a good lemon down!

jokes.j: Why was the potato so calm at the bottom of the bucket?
What is a rolling pin's favourite thing to do in water?
Why did the orange take off its peel?
jokes.a: It wanted to see how deep the water was!

jokes.j: What did the ice cube say to the spoon?
jokes.a: I'll stay cool on top, you go down and explore.

jokes.j: Why did the coconut never worry about the sea?
jokes.a: She always kept her head above water!

jokes.j: Why was the steel spoon bad at hide and seek in the bucket?
jokes.a: It always went straight to the bottom of the list.

maths.problem: In the bucket test, Revathi made 10 guesses. Draw a tally mark for each right guess: rolling pin wrong, coin wrong, lemon right, potato right, spoon right, bottle cap right, apple right, key right, ice right, candle wrong. How many were right? How many were wrong?
maths.explain: Count the tally marks: 7 right. 10 take away 7 is 3 wrong. Her wrong guesses were the rolling pin, the coin and the candle. Two of them were the heavy-or-light surprises.
maths.context: This question is about the bucket test. You guess, then put ten things from the kitchen into a bucket of water, one at a time, to see which float and which sink.
maths.why_maths: Tally marks show quickly how many guesses were right, and the wrong ones point to what surprised us.

maths.problem: Sort these made-up results into two columns, float and sink, and draw a block for each: rolling pin floated, coin sank, lemon floated, potato sank, spoon sank, cap floated, apple floated, key sank, ice floated, candle floated. Which column is taller? What are most of the sinkers made of?
maths.answer: Float has 6 blocks and sink has 4, so float is taller. Most of the sinkers are metal: the coin, the spoon and the key.
maths.explain: 6 is more than 4. Looking at the sink column shows a pattern: three of the four sinkers are metal. The fourth is the potato.
maths.context: This question is about the bucket test. You guess, then put ten things from the kitchen into a bucket of water, one at a time, to see which float and which sink.
maths.why_maths: Sorting into columns helps us spot a pattern in what sank.

maths.problem: Made-up numbers: Anjali put her rolling pin on one side of a homemade balance, and coins on the other. It took 60 coins to balance the rolling pin. Which is heavier, the rolling pin or one coin? The rolling pin floated and one coin sank. What does that tell you?
maths.answer: The rolling pin is heavier: as heavy as 60 coins. Yet it floated and a coin sank, so weight does not decide floating.
maths.explain: 60 coins balance one rolling pin, so the rolling pin is much heavier than one coin. If heavy things always sank, the rolling pin would sink first. It did not.
maths.context: This question is about Heavy in the Hand. You compare how heavy things feel, then see if heavy things sink.
maths.why_maths: Comparing weights with coins shows how much heavier the rolling pin is, which makes its floating even more surprising.

maths.problem: A grown-up cuts a potato in half. Then she cuts each half in half again. How many pieces are there now? If the whole potato sank, how many of the pieces will sink? What if she cuts each piece in half once more?
maths.answer: 4 pieces, and all 4 will sink. Cut again, there are 8 pieces, and all 8 will sink.
maths.explain: 1 potato makes 2 halves, and 2 halves make 4 quarters. Every piece is still potato, and potato sinks, so every piece sinks. 4 pieces cut in half make 8.
maths.context: This question is about the bucket test. You guess, then put ten things from the kitchen into a bucket of water, one at a time, to see which float and which sink.
maths.why_maths: Counting the pieces lets us predict the result for every one of them, because cutting changes the size but not the material.

warmup.a: A lemon, a rolling pin, a coconut, an ice cube, a leaf.
A coin, a steel spoon, a key, a potato, a stone.

warmup.q: Does a heavy thing always sink?
warmup.a: No. A heavy rolling pin or a coconut floats.

warmup.q: Does a tiny piece of potato float?
warmup.a: No. It sinks, like the whole potato.
The push of water upwards on anything put into it.

warmup.q: Why does a whole orange float?
warmup.a: Its peel is full of tiny air pockets.

roots.context: We have guessed and tested what floats and what sinks, cut a potato small, and peeled an orange. Now we ask what floating tells us about things, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In your test, the heavy wooden rolling pin floated and the light coin sank. A tiny piece of potato sank, just like the whole potato. So size and weight alone do not decide if a thing floats. For a solid lump, what it is made of decides.
deep_truth.habit: We judge things by how big they look and how heavy they feel in the hand. The bucket test showed that floating depends on the material all the way through, which the hand cannot feel.
deep_truth.evidence: In the bucket test, the heaviest thing, the rolling pin, floated, and one of the lightest, the coin, sank. A fingernail-sized piece of potato sank, and a matchstick floated like the rolling pin.

three.who_am_i: Your body is almost exactly as heavy as the same amount of water. Breathe in deeply, and the air in your lungs helps you float.
three.what_is_life: A coconut floats across the sea and grows into a palm on a new island. Floating is one way life travels.
three.what_is_this_world: The same water holds up a bamboo coracle on the Kaveri and a floating island on Loktak Lake, and lets a clay idol sink in Mumbai.

roots.thread: On the kitchen floor, a coin, a rolling pin and a potato look like three separate things. In the bucket, one water meets all of them, and each meets the water in its own way. The answer comes from what each thing is made of, all the way through, down to its tiniest particles. Everything is conscious, and each material has its own way of meeting the water.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha told the Kalama people not to believe something only because it is often said, or because it seems right. When you know for yourselves, he said, then accept it.
teachings.link: Many people say heavy things sink. You did not just believe it. You tested it, and the rolling pin floated.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4, the blind men and the elephant
teachings.teaching: Some blind men each touched one part of an elephant. One felt the leg and said an elephant is like a pillar. One felt the ear and said it is like a winnowing basket. Each was sure, and each knew only one part.
teachings.link: Your hand knew only one part of the rolling pin: how heavy it is. The bucket showed another part, what it is made of. You needed both to understand it.

teachings.teaching: Nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water. Yet nothing is better at overcoming what is hard and strong.
teachings.link: Soft water, which you can pour through your fingers, held up a heavy wooden rolling pin and a whole coconut.

science.text: Archimedes' rule: a floating thing sinks into the water until it has pushed aside water as heavy as itself.
Water presses harder the deeper you go. So it pushes harder on the bottom of a thing than on its top, and that difference is upthrust.

other_view.view: They say water, wood and coins have no awareness at all. They explain floating fully with weight and the push of the water, and they find no need for a mind to explain it.

practice.title: Float on your breath
practice.say: Lie down on your back on the floor. Put one hand on your chest. Breathe in slowly and deeply. Feel your chest rise. Now breathe out slowly. Feel it fall. Do this three times. In water, a big breath in helps a person float. The air inside you makes you lighter for your size.
practice.kid: Lie on your back. Put a hand on your chest. Breathe in slowly. Feel it rise. Breathe out. Do it three times.

ask: The rolling pin felt heavy, but it floated. What else might feel one way and be another way?
If you could choose, would you rather be a floater or a sinker? Why?
Your hand and the bucket told you different things. When two tests disagree, which one do you trust?

science: Archimedes, On Floating Bodies, Book 1, Proposition 5: a solid lighter than a fluid sinks until the weight of fluid it displaces equals its own weight.
The Archimedes Palimpsest: overwritten as a prayer book in 1229, identified by J. L. Heiberg in 1906, studied at the Walters Art Museum, Baltimore, from 1999, with conservation led by Abigail Quandt.
The Eureka story comes from Vitruvius, De Architectura, Book 9, written in the 1st century BCE.
Agnes Pockels, Surface Tension, Nature 43 (1891), a letter sent by Lord Rayleigh.
Potato specific gravity is about 1.06 to 1.10, so raw potatoes sink in plain water. Most woods, paraffin wax and polypropylene bottle caps are less dense than water.
Apples are about one quarter air by volume, and float. Orange peel has many air spaces, and peeled oranges usually sink.
Coconuts float and can stay able to grow after long times at sea, which helped them spread across tropical coasts.
Seed sorting by flotation: full seeds usually sink, empty or damaged seeds float.
Phumdis and Keibul Lamjao National Park, Loktak Lake, Manipur, home of the sangai deer. The Ithai barrage was built in the early 1980s.
The Pesse canoe, the Netherlands, about 10,000 years old. People reached Australia by sea more than 50,000 years ago.
Anguttara Nikaya 3.65 (Kalama Sutta). Udana 6.4 (Tittha Sutta). Tao Te Ching 78.

playtest: Thought through as a parent and child in a flat. Every material is in most Indian kitchens, and a bucket half full of water fits on a towel on the floor. The bucket test works because each thing is pushed down and let go, so nothing rests on the water's skin. Expected results: wooden rolling pin, lemon, apple, ice cube, candle, matchstick and most bottle caps float. Coin, steel spoon, key and raw potato sink, and so does a fingernail-sized piece of potato. A note covers a marble or steel rolling pin, and a bottle cap that fills with water. The orange test usually gives a slow sink once peeled, with a note to peel off more pith if not. The spine is the intro, Heavy in the Hand and the bucket test (session 1, about 35 minutes), then the explanations, Roots and the quiz (session 2, about 30 minutes). There is no Class 1 unit on this subtopic, so it leads on from the Class 2 solids, liquids and gases unit. It does not use the bottle with coins and air (the Class 2 adaptations unit), foil boats or coin rafts, salt water, clay boats or ships, which the Class 4 and 5 floating units and other units use.
